did.abstract: This collection consists of materials collected and created for an oral history project and subsequent exhibitions documenting the different ethnic and religious communities within Crown Heights, particularly the neighborhood's Jewish, Black, and Caribbean residents, and the racial tensions existing between them in the wake of the 1991 riots.
did.langmaterial: Collection materials are in English, Hebrew, Yiddish, and Haitian Creole.

bioghist.head: Historical Note
bioghist.p: The materials in this collection encompass an oral history project and exhibitions that were part of a joint effort between the Brooklyn Historical Society, the Brooklyn's Children Museum, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford-Stuyvesant History (now Weeksville Heritage Center) to document the different ethnic and religious communities within Crown Heights. The project focused on the neighborhood's Jewish, Black, and Caribbean residents, and the racial tensions existing between them in the wake of the August 1991 riots that erupted after seven-year-old Guyanese American Gavin Cato was struck and killed by a car in Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson's motorcade and resulted in the murder of Jewish scholar Yankel Rosenbaum and Italian-American Anthony Graziosi. The three organizations collaborated to capture perspectives on the racial unrest and discrimination before and after the riots, and how ethnic and religious communities attempted reconciliation during the years following the violence.

The project, first named "Bridging Eastern Parkway" but renamed "The Crown Heights History Project" (CHHP) in 1993, had two directors: cultural anthropologist Jill Vexler and historian Craig Wilder. The pair, aided by CHHP research assistant and Crown Heights resident Aviva Segall, conducted the majority of the interviews for the oral history portion of the project. The interviewers collected thirty-three oral histories with residents of varying religious and ethnic backgrounds, including members of Chabad Lubavitch, Orthodox and secular Jews, Black Americans, and Caribbean Americans, not only to examine the lead-up to and aftermath of the riots but also to document the lives, religious and cultural practices, and everyday experiences of the neighborhood's diverse population.

After completing the oral history portion of the project, Vexler, Wilder, and CHHP staff began collecting materials and compiling donations for exhibition display. Crown Heights residents donated materials and objects that reflected their unique cultural, religious, and personal experiences, and CHHP collected materials related to the neighborhood, its history, and the recent unrest. CHHP also contracted photographers Rodney Hurley, Miriam Rubinoff, and Chris Maynard to take photos for the exhibitions, and collected photographs from Myrtle Whitmore's collection for display.

The project culminated in three exhibitions, one hosted by each organization: BHS's Crown Heights: Perceptions and Realities, Brooklyn Children's Museum's Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford-Stuyvesant's Crown Heights: The African Diaspora, all of which opened in spring of 1994.
Sources: Rule, Sheila. "The Voices and Faces of Crown Heights." New York Times (New York, NY), April 15, 1994.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This collection contains oral histories, print materials, and photographs collected and donated for exhibitions documenting the ethnic and religious communities of Brooklyn's Crown Heights neighborhood in the years following the Crown Heights Riots in August 1991.

Project staff conducted thirty-three oral history interviews, originally recorded on portable cassette tapes, to document the experiences of Jewish, Black, and Caribbean residents of Crown Heights. These oral histories contain descriptions of family and heritage; immigration and relocation; cultural and racial relations; occupations and professions; education and religion; housing and gentrification; civil unrest and reconciliation; media representation and portrayal; and community activism.

Materials donated to and collected by CHHP staff include flyers, brochures, and posters for cultural, religious, and community organizations; West Indian American Day Carnival ephemera; religious literature; personal letters; invitations; business cards; advertisements; and a substantial number of newspaper clippings and magazines.

The CHHP hired photographers to document the cultural and religious lives of Crown Heights residents. The collection's photographic materials include 252 prints, 324 photographic negatives, 80 35mm slides, and 66 photographic contact sheets. Subjects include church and synagogue services, storefronts and homes in Crown Heights, Chabad Lubavitch gatherings, religious holidays, familial gatherings, and neighborhood residents.

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: Recordings and transcripts were collected through the Crown Heights History Project, a collaboration among the Brooklyn Historical Society, the Brooklyn Children's Museum, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford Stuyvesant History (now Weeksville Heritage Center). The curator and one of the project's directors, Jill Vexler, retained the project records. Brooklyn Historical Society acquired the collection from Vexler in 2012.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Recordings and transcripts were digitized by the Brooklyn Historical Society in 2015. Due to privacy concerns, the processing archivists redacted specific dates of birth of all narrators or other named individuals from the digitized transcripts and audio recordings. The Crown Heights History Project oral histories were processed by Brett Dion, Nilaja Troy, Joe Teutonico, and Harunobu Coryne. Olivia Mastrosimone, Project Archivist, processed the remaining collection materials and reprocessed the oral histories in 2026.

Folder titles in brackets were provided by Olivia Mastrosimone. The archivist moved administrative materials and photo duplicates from this collection to Brooklyn Historical Society institutional records (ARC.288), and discarded additional digital copies of oral history interviews and transcripts.

odd.head: Oral History Note
odd.p: Oral history interviews are intimate conversations between two people, both of whom have generously agreed to share these recordings with the Center for Brooklyn History archives and with researchers. Please listen in the spirit with which these were shared. Researchers will understand that:

1. The Center for Brooklyn History abides by the General Principles & Best Practices for Oral History as agreed upon by the Oral History Association (2009) and expects that use of this material will be done with respect for these professional ethics.

2. Every oral history relies on the memories, views, and opinions of the narrator. Because of the personal nature of oral history, listeners may find some viewpoints or language of the recorded participants to be objectionable. In keeping with its mission of preservation and unfettered access whenever possible, CBH presents these views as recorded.

3. Transcripts created prior to 2008 serve as a guide to the interview and are not considered verbatim. The audio recording should be considered the primary source for each interview. It may contain natural false starts, verbal stumbles, misspeaks, repetitions that are common in conversation, and other passages and phrases omitted from the transcript. This decision was made because CBH gives primacy to the audible voice and also because some researchers do find useful information in these verbal patterns.

4. Unless these verbal patterns are germane to your scholarly work, when quoting from this material, researchers are encouraged to correct the grammar and make other modifications, maintaining the flavor of the narrator's speech while editing the material for the standards of print.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Rev. Dr. A.R. Bernard was born in Panama City, Panama, in 1953. At the age of four, he and his mother, Adelina Fleming, an Olympic track star, immigrated to the United States. Rev. Bernard grew up in the Bedford-Stuyvesant and Bushwick neighborhoods of Brooklyn, where he attended public schools. He was bused to Ridgewood, Queens, in the 1960s to attend junior high and high school. Impacted by the racism and segregation he experienced, Rev. Dr. Bernard became interested in the Black Panthers and a follower of the Nation of Islam. On January 11, 1975, he became a Christian. At the time of the 1993 interview, he was ministering to 625 families in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. Focused on a conservative, family-centered, practical faith, Rev. Dr. Bernard is, as of 2026, the senior pastor of the Christian Cultural Center located at 1400 Linden Boulevard, Brooklyn, New York.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Dr. Rev. A.R. Bernard discusses his childhood in Brooklyn, his experience with the Civil Rights Movement and the Nation of Islam, and his reasons for converting to Christianity. He remembers racial conflicts, violence, and the institutional segregation of the 1950s and 1960s. He reflects on the Black awareness that the Black Panthers and the Nation of Islam provided in the community during this period and relates this to his conversion experience. The interview concludes with a focus on the mission, makeup, and contributions of the Christian Life Center. He shares his views on what he sees as a breakdown of family and community, offering solutions aligned with the church's focus. He responds to questions concerning the riot of 1991 in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Chaim Burston

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Chaim Burston

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Chaim Burston was born to Jewish-American parents in Pasadena, California. After enrolling at Tel Aviv University, Chaim traveled to Israel. After joining a Lubavitch Hasidic community as a baal teshuvah (a Jew returning to Orthodoxy), Burston returned to the United States to continue his studies in New York. It was in the Lubavitch community of Crown Heights, Brooklyn, where he met his wife Chana. The young couple married, purchased a home—and with Chaim becoming an elementary school teacher along the way—had eight children together. A musician, Burston had taken to playing melodies intended to accompany prayers.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Burston recounts his youth, his travels to Israel, and his rediscovery of his religion. He also discusses meeting his wife, what it's like raising a large family in New York City, and touches on relations with his Afro-Caribbean neighbors in the aftermath of the 1991 riot in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. The interview ends with Burston playing his synthesizer keyboard. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Rachel Lea Cattan, a Jewish resident of Crown Heights, was born to Polish parents in Novosibirsk, Siberia, in the former Soviet Union. At the age of eleven, her parents moved the family to Lodz, Poland, and a year later to Braslav. Then, at age thirteen, the family immigrated to the United States, settling in the East New York neighborhood of Brooklyn. Cattan attended New York public schools, including the Music and Art High School (now Fiorella H. LaGuardia High School). She completed her undergraduate degree in painting at the Pratt Institute. At the time of the 1993 interview, she was a public school teacher in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn and a divorced mother of four.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Cattan discusses her childhood, immigration to the United States, her transition to an observant Jewish lifestyle, her divorce, and the racial tensions of the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. Interview conducted by Aviva Segall.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Avroham Crawford

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Avroham Crawford

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Avroham Crawford grew up in the Sunset Park neighborhood of Brooklyn, the son of Irish-Catholic immigrants from Newfoundland. He was raised in the church, but considered converting to Judaism while studying for his bachelor's degree in philosophy at NYU, where he worked as a librarian at the time of this interview. He moved to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights in 1970 and, shortly afterward, converted to Orthodox Judaism with assistance from Rabbi Yisroel Jacobson. He chose the Jewish name "Avroham" at this time. In 1975, he married Suri Perlman, and they had three children: Nechama, Yitzhak, and Yisroel. He died in 2011.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Avroham Crawford, in his late 40s, narrates his Irish Catholic upbringing, his early encounters with Jewish people, and his conversion to Orthodox Judaism. He describes how the Lubavitch community in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn has changed and grown in the years since he first moved there in 1970. He reflects on the religious community's acceptance of him as a Christian convert, on how his children have grown up Lubavitch, and on secular Jews who take up Orthodox practice as adults (known as baal teshuvah). When asked, he explains the extent of his interaction with the Black residents of Crown Heights. At various points throughout the interview, he dwells on religious subjects: how boys and girls are educated, how Judaism differs from Christianity, and how conversion for marriage differs from conversion for faith alone. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

did.unittitle: Crawford, Nechama, Yisroel Crawford and Suri Crawford

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Nechama Crawford was raised in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. She attended a private Lubavitch school, Bais Rivkah, from kindergarten through twelfth grade. At her Bat Mitzvah, she read from the Genesis chapter Chayei Sarah, or "The Life of Sarah." Her younger brother, Yisroel, attended Oholei Torah—a Lubavitch school that focuses on religious education and teaches exclusively in Hebrew and Yiddish—before switching to Lubavitch Yeshiva. Their mother, Suri, grew up in Holyoke, Massachusetts, and had a Modern Orthodox upbringing among her Litvish (Latvian Jewish) family.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Nechama and Yisroel—respectively in twelfth and sixth grade at the time of the interview—talk about their experience growing up in the Lubavitch community of the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. They describe the various forms of religious education and practice within Hasidic Judaism, as well as the expectations and roles laid out for young girls and boys. Nechama reflects on her community's relationship with the "outside," especially the Black residents of Crown Heights and the non-Jewish residents of the rest of New York City. Suri, their mother, talks about her children's education, the role of women in her religion, the cost of living in Brooklyn, and her Modern Orthodox upbringing. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Roxanne De Shong

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Roxanne De Shong

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Roxanne De Shong was born in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. She immigrated to Brooklyn in the 1970s with her parents and settled on Crown Street in the Crown Heights neighborhood. Her father sold life insurance and her mother worked near the family home at Woolworth's. She went to a public school in the East New York neighborhood of Brooklyn for one year, then to Holy Spirit Catholic School for grades two to eight. She attended Clara Barton High School and then Hostoff's in The Bronx. De Shong studied to become a Dental Assistant in high school and worked at several offices in New York City. De Shong has children, including one son whose father was shot and killed in a drug-related incident in the Harlem neighborhood of Manhattan, which she mentioned in her interview.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, De Shong discusses the cultural differences between Caribbean- and American-born people, the stereotypes associated with West Indians and Jamaicans, and the changes in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn from when she arrived in the 1970s to the time of the interview in 1993. She specifically notes the presence of crime, violence, and drugs. The two also discussed misperceptions between the Lubavitch and Black residents, and what she perceives to be inequities in housing and safety, as well as the struggle to live in Crown Heights and her son's relationship with Gavin Cato. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Esther Goldman

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Esther Goldman

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Esther Goldman was born in Poland in 1926. An observant Jew from birth, she came to New York with her mother and siblings in 1934, joining her father, who had arrived two years earlier. After living in the East New York neighborhood of Brooklyn for several years, Goldman's family moved to Eastern Parkway in the Crown Heights neighborhood in 1941. After marrying and briefly living in Philadelphia, Goldman returned to Crown Heights with her husband, and they had four children together. With Goldman's children grown and out of the house, she began working for a company on Broadway and Spring Street in Manhattan.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Esther Goldman discusses her upbringing in Poland, East New York, and on Eastern Parkway in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. She recalls the growing Lubavitch movement of the mid- to late twentieth century, and traces her own life's journey through discussions on faith, family, neighbors, white flight, and historic events. She ends with a discussion about the 1991 Crown Heights riot and its aftermath. Interview conducted by Aviva Segall.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Joseph Harold Haynes

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Joseph Harold Haynes

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Joseph Harold Haynes grew up in the Bedford-Stuyvesant and Crown Heights neighborhoods of Brooklyn. He attended Haaren High School for aviation studies and received a degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Missouri. Haynes was employed as a mechanical engineer for the New York City Transit Authority and as an accident investigator for the National Transportation Safety Board. He was a licensed commercial pilot and flight instructor. A contributor to the now-defunct New Museum Community Museum, Haynes was a founding member of the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville. Haynes was in his 60s at the time of his interview. He died March 2, 1997.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Haynes discusses growing up in central Brooklyn during the 1940s and '50s, the importance of family, racial segregation, his passion for aviation, the Muse Community Museum, the founding of the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville, the 1991 riot in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights, and the future of race relations. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Iyedun Ince

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Iyedun Ince

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: At the time of the 1993 interview, Iyedun Ince, an African-American resident of Crown Heights, was twenty years old. Born in Harlem, New York, he and his brother Ojo Ashegun were raised by a single mother in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. He attended parochial and public schools in the area and graduated from Brooklyn Technical High School. As of 2016, Iyedun is a djembe musician and teacher in New York City.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The narrator discusses his childhood in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights, his disillusionment in high school, and the decline of the youth culture in Crown Heights. He describes his own struggle to define himself and free himself from the pressures of his generation. He discusses possible approaches to changing the neighborhood's social environment and concludes the interview with advice for the youth of Crown Heights. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Simon Jacobson

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Simon Jacobson

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Rabbi Simon Jacobson was born in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights in 1956. Observant from birth, he attended Lubavitch Yeshiva and lived on St. Marks Avenue before moving to Sullivan Place. His father was Gershon Jacobson, founder and publisher of the Yiddish-language Hasidic newspaper Der Algemeiner. For several years, Jacobson worked as the editor and translator of speeches by the Lubavitch Rebbe, Menachem Schneerson. Later, he became the director of Vaad Hanochos Hatmimim, a foundation that promotes Schneerson's teachings. A noted teacher in the community, he founded a Lubavitch organization for outreach and education called the Meaningful Life Center, based on Eastern Parkway.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Rabbi Simon Jacobson narrates his childhood in Crown Heights during the 1950s and '60s, recounting how the ethnic and religious composition of the Brooklyn neighborhood (including among different Hasidic movements) has changed throughout his lifetime. He explains the religious reasons why the Lubavitch have stayed in Crown Heights when other Jewish groups have left, and he addresses various subjects related to home-ownership, including the role played by the Crown Heights Jewish Community Council and the perception that the Lubavitch want to drive Black and Caribbean residents out of the neighborhood. He describes the Lubavitch community's relationship with non-Jews and non-practicing Jews, dwelling on the concept of "chosenness." He and the interviewer discuss possible venues for outreach and cultural "translation," especially of Jewish holidays and the concept of Moshiach (or messiah). Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Baila Kamman

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Baila Kamman

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Baila Kamman was born in the Bronx, New York, to middle-class, secular Jewish parents. While on a summer vacation during her stint as a New York City public school teacher, she was traveling in Israel during the 1973 Arab-Israeli War. Kamman explains that the experience left her with a renewed interest in her religion. Opting to relocate to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights with a group of women seeking an Orthodox Jewish lifestyle, Kamman and her friends faced a steep learning curve as they tried to navigate the traditions and mores of their new community. She married and completed a law degree while raising five children. After briefly relocating to Rockland County, New York, in the late 1980s, Kamman and her husband were once again residing in Crown Heights in 1993.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Kamman, in her 40s, discusses her secular upbringing in a Bronx neighborhood filled with both Reform and Orthodox Jews, her college years in Queens, and her life as a young public elementary school teacher during the 1970s. She recounts the experience of being in Israel during the 1973 Arab-Israeli War and the steps leading up to her eventual entry into the world of Lubavitch Hasidism, as well as how this new conservative lifestyle contradicted many of her personal values. Kamman also details the courtship that led to her marriage, remembers escalating racial tensions leading up to the Crown Heights neighborhood riot of 1991, and explains how her father's death inspired her to attain a law degree while raising five children. Interview conducted by Aviva Segall.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Zalman Kleinman

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Zalman Kleinman was born in 1933 in Leningrad, the former Soviet Union, to a Lubavitch family. After the death of his parents, he and his sister were sent to Siberia, where a rabbi adopted him. For a time he lived amongst the Bukharian Jews in Samarkand. Kleinman immigrated to Paris, where he studied at an underground Lubavitch yeshiva. From Paris, he traveled to Israel, where he began painting. He returned to Paris, where he met and married his wife Rosa. In 1958, they immigrated to New York City and to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. Kleinman was an illustrator and artist known for painting Hasidic life. He died in 1995.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents

Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Carlos Lezama

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Carlos Lezama

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Carlos Lezama was born in 1923 in Coro, Venezuela. He grew up in Trinidad but later returned to Venezuela, where he was an auto worker for General Motors and Chrysler, as well as a mechanic in Caracas specializing in dental machinery. After that, he departed for a job as a merchant mariner. It was during his travels as a seaman that he first visited the United States and eventually resolved to move to New York City, which he did, alone, in 1954. He had lived in Manhattan for about two years when he moved to Crown Heights after noticing the greater movement of Caribbean people into the neighborhood. Soon after his move, his wife and children joined him. They were all congregants at Saint Gregory Catholic Church. He continued to work as a mechanic, taking vocational courses to supplement his training, and bought a home on St. Johns Place. During this time, he became a prominent figure in the cultural life of the West Indian residents of Crown Heights.

Along with Rufus (Lionel) Gorin, he was a key organizer of the first Carnival parade on Eastern Parkway, now commonly known as the West Indian American Day Parade, in 1969. When Gorin died, Lezama was elected the first president of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), a position he held until his retirement in 2002. He died in 2007.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Lezama spends much of his narration recounting the many years he has lived in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. He describes his life in Venezuela as a young man, his experience of moving to New York on his own, and the steps he took toward settlement and eventual homeownership. He relates the personal facts of his life to the observations he has made about Caribbean immigrants in general, and he compares the openness of the present-day West Indian community to the more isolated environment that he encountered when he first arrived in the 1950s. In particular, he describes an improvement in relations between West Indian immigrants and American-born Black people (an increasing number of whom, he notes, are from the southern United States). He tells the history of the Labor Day Carnival (or West Indian Day Parade), which he had been leading for twenty-six years. He notes that the parade has long been a source of tension and debate with the Hasidic Jews of Eastern Parkway, and he ascribes the 1991 unrest that erupted around the deaths of Gavin Cato and Yankel Rosenbaum, in part, to this tension. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Bracha Meshchaninov

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Bracha Meshchaninov was born in Johannesburg, South Africa. At fourteen, she began seeking a deeper connection to her Jewish faith and, at eighteen, traveled to Jerusalem to attend Neve Yerushalayim, an all-girls religious school. After graduating from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg with degrees in English, guidance counseling, and education, she returned to Israel. At twenty-two, Bracha traveled to the United States, where she studied with Lubavitch Hasidim. She soon dedicated herself to Yiddishkeit (a Yiddish word meaning "Jewishness") and married her husband Ilya. At the time of the 1993 interview, she was in her thirties and a photographer living in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. She now lives in Rockland County, New York, where she is an educator and Yoga teacher.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Bracha Meshchaninov discusses her childhood and family in Johannesburg, South Africa, her religious education in Israel, being a baal teshuvah (a Jew converted to Orthodoxy), her courtship and marriage to a Russian baal teshuvah, navigating a newly religious identity, the physical decline of the Rebbe and the spiritual ramifications within Lubavitch Hasidim, and moving from the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Rev. Dr. Clive Neil

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Born in Mandeville, Jamaica, in 1959, Rev. Dr. Clive E. Neil came to the United States on a soccer scholarship. He was an honors student at Eastern University and a fellow at Princeton University. He has a master's degree in Divinity and a doctorate in Counseling from Drew University. He was ordained and served as minister at Tremont Presbyterian Church in the Bronx from 1985 to 1988. His pastorship at Bedford-Central Presbyterian Church began in 1988. He has written three books, taught and lectured at area colleges, and enrolled as a Ministry Leadership Network scholar. Rev. Dr. Neil has two children. As of 2026, Rev. Dr. Neil is the Senior Pastor at the Bedford Central Presbyterian Church.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Rev. Dr. Clive E. Neil discusses the misperceptions and strengths of Jamaicans and Jamaican Americans. He recalls the hardship of leaving family and country, his time in higher education, and inner-city volunteer work. He describes the ethnic makeup of his congregation on the border of the Crown Heights and Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhoods of Brooklyn and how the diversity of these neighborhoods is both a tool for education and something to celebrate. Neil points out family and community causes he actively supports, such as a Men's Ministry at his church and the Nehemiah Homes effort. He also describes the transformation of the area's Black churches brought on by the influx of young ministers. He shares his views on the community turmoil and violence related to the deaths of Gavin Cato and Yankel Rosenbaum, the reaction of the local clergy, and what he feels to be unfair media coverage on the matter. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

dao.xlink:title: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Louvenia Pointer

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Louvenia Pointer

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Louvenia Pointer, a Black woman born in 1916 as Louvenia White, was raised in Holly Hill, South Carolina, until 1926. She then lived in Harlem and the Bronx in New York City while working as a professional pianist, organist, and soprano. She studied Music Education at New York University and was cast in many Broadway productions, working with artists and thespians including Noel Coward and Ossie Davis. Pointer directed the National Youth Administration Radio Workshop chorus in 1943. She married William Davis Pointer, Sr. in 1947. Moving to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights in 1954, they raised three children. Retired from the theater, Pointer worked as a music teacher in several Brooklyn schools as well as privately. She was active in civic affairs and participated in her block association and the Brooklyn Women's Coalition. She founded the Great Day Chorale, a touring a cappella group, in 1987. She died in 2009.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Louvenia Pointer says very little about her life before moving to the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. She recounts searching for and finding the Carroll Street home she and her husband bought. Race is discussed in the context of public schools and the neighborhood. She remembers the events that led her from teaching music privately to public education. Pointer describes her participation in the block association, past and present, as well as the neighborhood children, historically, and children in general. Finally, she talks about the flaws in people that can lead to neighborhood tension, and how best to heal that tension. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Reverend William D. Pointer, Jr. was born to William and Louvenia Pointer in New York City in 1952. He is married to Elder Lillie Pointer, who serves with him at the Christian Cultural Center (CCC). Since 1992, Rev. Pointer has served at CCC as Associate Pastor and Senior Elder, as well as the Director of the Performing Arts Ministry. He and his wife have traveled and ministered across the globe. In 2009, his book "Moving from Pain to Power" was published. As of 2026, Rev. Dr. Pointer is an Associate Pastor and Senior Elder at the CCC.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Reverend William D. Pointer, Jr. recalls his childhood, his relationship with his best friend from the Jewish family next door, and home ownership of different ethnic groups in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. He describes his activism as a teenager during the Black Power movement and how the African Student Association effected change. When describing the climate that led to the cultural turmoil in Crown Heights in 1991, Reverend Pointer looks to the differing ways the nation and its varying cultures value family and community. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Carl E. Roberts

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: A Jamaican American, Carl E. Roberts has lived in Brooklyn for all his adult life. He emigrated in 1954 while still in his teens, when his family moved to the Brooklyn neighborhood of Bedford-Stuyvesant. He worked full-time at a Macy's department store while attending Brooklyn College part-time. His family moved to the Crown Heights neighborhood in 1958. After serving in the Army for over two years, he took a job as a bank teller. Roberts, an Investment Banking major, completed his education at New York University. He went to work for New York Life Insurance and also started a tax consulting business at home with help from his wife. For much of the 1980s, Roberts was a local politician and community activist, serving on Community Board Nine and related committees. He ran three unsuccessful campaigns for a seat in the New York State Assembly.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Carl E. Roberts discusses misconceptions about Jamaicans and Jamaican Americans, his educational and professional experiences, and his community activism. He speaks directly about the real and perceived rifts between the Black communities and the Orthodox and Hasidim communities in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, and ways he thinks community members can improve relations. Roberts offers his insight into the changes in real estate ownership within Crown Heights over several decades and how these changes affect the neighborhood. Interview conducted by Craig Wilder.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Bella and Gabriel Rubaszkin

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Bella (Biela) Rubovzkin was born in 1933 in Krolevets, Ukraine. Observant from birth, she fled her home village as World War II intensified in 1941. She and her family migrated east to Saratov, Russia, and then further east until the war's end. She met her future husband, Gabriel Rubaszkin, a Russian Jew, in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Religious persecution forced their move to the United States after passing through several countries. During their five-year stay in France, Bella and Gabriel were married. They arrived in New York in 1954. By 1958, they had settled in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights and began raising a family. By 1993, they were grandparents. They sold their Carroll Street home in 2005 and have since resided in White Lake, New York, and Miami Beach, Florida.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Bella Rubovzkin discusses some traditions, teachings, and social practices of the Lubavitch community. She and her husband Gabriel talk about their displacement in Europe and Russia during and after World War II, the changing ethnicities of the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, changes in where Jews have settled in the New York City area since the 1950s, and job opportunities for their neighbors and relatives. They discuss their observations of the ethnic and racial tensions of Crown Heights from the 1970s through to the 1991 riots and beyond. Bella also offers her thoughts on the strife within the community and ways of reconciliation. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Aviva Segall grew up in Youngstown, Ohio, in a Conservative Jewish family. Aviva first became acquainted with Hasidism at a Lubavitch-sponsored youth event in her hometown at the age of fourteen. Four years later, Aviva met a Hasidic woman at a women's conference in Minnesota who invited Segall to attend her wedding in Crown Heights. She traveled to Brooklyn and formed her first impressions of the neighborhood. She eventually joined other formerly secular women as baal teshuvah (Jews who returned to Orthodoxy) and immersed herself in the Hasidic lifestyle of Crown Heights. Some years later, Segall got married and began a family with her husband. At the time of the 1993 interview, she was a research assistant on the Crown Heights History Project and a twenty-year resident of Crown Heights.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Aviva Segall discusses her first contacts with the Hasidic community as a teenager, the events that led to her joining the Lubavitch community, and the differences between her observant Conservative upbringing and her current Hasidic lifestyle. She examines the pros and cons of the secular and religious worlds, life as a baal teshuvah (Jews returned to Orthodoxy), cultural faux pas in the Orthodox enclave of the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, and the authority of the Lubavitch spiritual leader, or Rebbe. Race relations, neighborhood transitions, education, and politics are also discussed. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Devora Leah Shaffer-Slutzkin (Devori) grew up in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn, with her parents and nine siblings. She graduated from Beth Rivkah High School and, at eighteen, attended Beth Rivkah's teacher training seminary and Touro College. She visited international Lubavitch camps and served as a counselor at a Jewish summer camp in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. She married Reb Doron Slutzkin and resides in Zurich, Switzerland.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: In the interview, Shaffer talks about her day-to-day life as a Jewish Lubavitcher teenage girl, including her schooling, teacher training, camping experiences, and living in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights and New York City. Shaffer offers her thoughts on how the Lubavitch community coexists with non-Jewish people as well as other ethnic and racial minorities. She speaks of her own and her community's devotion to the Rebbe, how she may meet her future husband, the differences in being Hasidic and being religious, and her immediate reaction to the civil unrest in Crown Heights. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Martha Sacolick was born in 1931 on Eastern Parkway in Brooklyn to Polish Jews who had immigrated to the United States after World War II. In her childhood, the family resided on Herzl Street in Brooklyn and then Stanton Street in Manhattan. She attended P.S. 65, graduated from Seward Park High School, and then took accounting courses. As an adult, she lived in the Brooklyn neighborhoods of Williamsburg and Borough Park. She met her husband, Shimshon Stock, while working at a belt manufacturer in the early 1950s, and they married in Borough Park. Stock was born into an Orthodox family in New York City in 1929. In his childhood, the family resided in the Rockaway Beach and Brownsville neighborhoods. He and Martha first shared a home in East New York, and in 1964, they settled in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. Stock was a community leader, working closely with the Lubavitch Rebbe on several occasions. The couple had a son and two daughters, and over a dozen grandchildren. Martha and Shimshon Stock died in 2007.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Martha Stock discusses the experience of growing up Lubavitcher and receiving a secular education. She talks about her parents' meeting and the experiences of family members who left Poland during World War II. Her husband, Shimshon, joins Martha in the interview. They review the issues of home ownership in the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights. Martha and Shimshon discuss their intolerance for their African American neighbors and non-Jewish cultures. Stock describes the struggle and frustration of anti-Semitism and the Hasidic community's separatism within society. He takes issue with his own community and local, state, and national politics. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

daodesc.p: Oral History Interview (Audio) with Dellon A. Wilson

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Dellon Wilson was born in Saint Anne, Jamaica, and raised in Kingston. In her pre-teens, Wilson moved to Westchester County, New York. After graduating from White Plains High School, she enlisted in the United States Army. After serving, she attended New York University and Hunter College, where she completed an undergraduate degree in Theatre and Film Production and a master's degree in Biology. In 1980, Wilson moved in to an apartment on Eastern Parkway in the Crown Heights neighborhood of Brooklyn. She worked as forensic medicine microbiologist in a Medical Examiner's office for eight years. After taking leave from full-time employment due to a job-related illness, Wilson volunteered her time to women's rights and AIDS-related causes. She died in September, 1995.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Dellon Wilson, a Jamaican American, discusses her upbringing, training in the Army, schooling in the United States, and an illness that forced her to stop working. She shares her perspectives on racial tolerance and intolerance, relates personal experiences of feeling unfairly judged in her teens, her contemporary viewpoint on the racial and ethnic makeup of the Brooklyn neighborhood of Crown Heights community, and the media's portrayal of the riots after the auto accident that killed Gavin Cato in Crown Heights. Interview conducted by Jill Vexler.

bioghist.head: Biographical Note
bioghist.p: Carlos Lezama was born in 1923 in Coro, Venezuela. He grew up in Trinidad but later returned to Venezuela, where he was an auto worker for General Motors and Chrysler, as well as a mechanic in Caracas specializing in dental machinery. After that, he departed for a job as a merchant mariner. It was during his travels as a seaman that he first visited the United States and eventually resolved to move to New York City, which he did, alone, in 1954. He had lived in Manhattan for about two years when he moved to Crown Heights after noticing the greater movement of Caribbean people into the neighborhood. While living in Crown Heights he became a prominent figure in the cultural life of the neighborhood's West Indian residents.

Along with Rufus (Lionel) Gorin, he was a key organizer of the first Carnival parade on Eastern Parkway, now commonly known as the West Indian American Day Parade, in 1969. When Gorin died, Lezama was elected the first president of the West Indian American Day Carnival Association (WIADCA), a position he held until his retirement in 2002. He died in 2007.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Sub-series 4.1: Rodney Hurley photographs, c.1990s, includes 30 black & white 4x6 prints, 55 8x10 prints, 40 photographic contact sheets, and 101 photographic negatives taken by Hurley for BHS's Crown Heights: Perceptions and Realities, Brooklyn Children's Museum's Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford-Stuyvesant's Crown Heights: The African Diaspora exhibitions. The Crown Heights History Project hired Hurley to photograph religious and community events in Crown Heights, as well as Crown Heights residents, streets, and storefronts. Hurley also photographed oral history interviewees, shots of whom are interspersed throughout the prints and contact sheets.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This sub-series is arranged by format, and the prints, contact sheets, and negatives are arranged in order according to the photographer's shot list, which can be found in the accession log.

otherfindaid.head: Other Finding Aids
otherfindaid.p: Some photographic prints are labeled and correspond to a shot list, which can be found in the accession log.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Sub-series 4.2: Miriam Rubinoff photographs, 1994, includes 16 4x6 prints, 99 8x10 prints, 6 5x7 prints, 12 photographic contact sheets, 84 negatives, and 28 35mm slides taken by Rubinoff for BHS's Crown Heights: Perceptions and Realities, Brooklyn Children's Museum's Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford-Stuyvesant's Crown Heights: The African Diaspora exhibitions. The Crown Heights History Project hired Rubinoff to photograph the neighborhood's Jewish residents, especially the Chabad Lubavitch community, including religious, community, and familial gatherings, as well as houses, storefronts, streets, and religiously significant objects. Rubinoff also photographed the opening of BHS's exhibition in 1994.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: This sub-series is arranged by subject and format. The prints and negatives are arranged in order according to shot numbers on the contact sheets.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Sub-series 4.4: Chris Maynard photographs, c.1993, consists of 11 photographic contact sheets taken by Chris Maynard for the Brooklyn Children's Museum's Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop exhibition in 1994. The sub-series includes photos of Jewish and Christian gatherings and religious services in Crown Heights. The contact sheets in this sub-series have handwritten notes on the back by the photographer.

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: The Brooklyn Children's Museum commissioned Chris Maynard to take photographs for their 1994 exhibition, Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop. The BCM donated Maynard's photographs to the Brooklyn Historical Society in 1995.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Sub-series 4.5: Additional photographers, 1994, includes 21 4x6 prints, 4 8x10 prints, 2 photographic contact sheets, and 130 negatives taken for BHS's Crown Heights: Perceptions and Realities, Brooklyn Children's Museum's Crown Heights: The Inside Scoop, and the Society for the Preservation of Weeksville and Bedford-Stuyvesant's Crown Heights: The African Diaspora exhibitions. These photographs include photos of community events, exterior shots of homes in Crown Heights, and shots of police confrontations.
